title: Unveiling Mucorales infections: A cutting-edge longitudinal imaging approach for real-time infection and host-response monitoring in Galleria mellonella and mouse models

paragraphs.en: Mucormycosis, caused by fungi of the Mucorales order, manifests in various clinical forms, including devastating pulmonary and rhino-orbital-cerebral infections. These often require surgical intervention involving the removal of facial and bone tissue, leading to profound life-changing morbidities and high mortality rates [1–6]. The most common genera associated with human disease are Rhizopus, Mucor, Lichtheimia and Rhizomucor [1,7]. The incidence of Mucorales infections is rising, with an estimated mean annual occurrence of 211,000 cases and mortality in untreated invasive fungal disease remains close to 100% [1,8,9]. This is concerning not only for immunocompromised populations such as hematologic and solid organ transplant patients, but also for other at-risk groups, including patients with diabetes mellitus or iron anomalies [5] which are more strongly linked to mucormycosis than to other invasive fungal diseases (IFD). Moreover, mucormycosis has been documented in multiple cases among influenza and COVID-19 patients, likely related to virus-host responses and corticosteroid therapies, with reported mortality rates ranging from 15% to 90% [10–12]. It also represents one of the few invasive fungal infections that can affect immunocompetent individuals, particularly in the context of severe burns, traumatic injuries, or combat wounds [13–15].

Overall, Mucorales fungi are generally resistant to most antifungal agents, resulting in a markedly limited therapeutic arsenal compared to other fungal pathogens. Available treatment options are restricted mainly to liposomal amphotericin B, posaconazole, and isavuconazole [2,16]. Furthermore, treatment with the available antifungals is limited by renal toxicity, prolonged and costly regimens, challenges with routes of administration, and significant drug–drug interactions [17]. The unacceptably high mortality rates associated with mucormycosis reflect not only the aggressive nature of the infection and the limitations of current antifungals but also highlight the inability of the immune system to effectively prevent or clear the infection. The reported alarming outcomes underscore the urgent need for a better understanding of mucormycosis host–pathogen interactions and the development of novel therapeutic and prophylactic strategies. As such, the World Health Organization has recognized mucormycosis infections as a global threat and the urgency of these priorities, calling for increased awareness and collaborative interdisciplinary efforts (One Health approach) to mitigate the emergence of the disease and development of preventive-therapeutic strategies [18].

In vivo preclinical studies have been pivotal for studying mucormycosis infections and evaluating antifungal strategies [19], providing valuable translational insights that enhance their applicability to clinical studies. An effective preclinical research platform should integrate various models, including in vitro and in vivo models. However, the currently available state-of-the-art experimental models remain insufficient, as they lack innovation, standardization, or reproducibility. Moreover, these models rely mainly on invasive single-timepoint readouts, such as colony-forming unit (CFU) counting and histology, which have inherent variability and require sacrificing several animals at multiple experimental timepoints to obtain a more comprehensive picture of disease progression. CFU counting is particularly challenging for Mucorales, as their coenocytic hyphae (characterized by a continuous multinucleate cytoplasm lacking septa) are highly susceptible to mechanical disruption during tissue homogenization, and fragmentation of these multinucleate segments results in loss of viability, likely leading to inaccurate and variable fungal burden estimates [20]. The few available longitudinal readouts focus on animal survival rates and health scoring systems. While these data provide insight into health deterioration observed over time in infected individuals, they do not clarify whether this decline results directly from the infection, nor do they fully capture the complexity of disease, limiting our understanding of host and pathogen interactions over time. In addition, the subjective nature of qualitative readouts introduces inter-observer variability, hampering reproducibility and cross-study interpretation.

Therefore, there is a critical need for innovative disease models, methodologies and analytical readouts to overcome current limitations and enable longitudinal tracking of disease progression and host–pathogen interactions over time, particularly in models that simulate mucormycosis-predisposing conditions in patients. Noninvasive modalities, such as bioluminescence (BL) or micro-CT imaging, enable longitudinal monitoring of individual animals, providing real-time insights into fungal burden kinetics and host-induced disease development, respectively. These approaches allow for repeated assessments at multiple time points, thereby increasing sensitivity and enhancing our understanding of the disease over time. Such imaging modalities and strategies have been successfully applied in studying other fungi, including Aspergillus fumigatus and Cryptococcus neoformans [21–23]. Furthermore, by preventing the need to sacrifice animals at different time points, these approaches align with the principles of the 3Rs (Reduction, Replacement and Refinement) in promoting ethically humane animal research [21,23–28].

To address these key existing gaps in mucormycosis research, we developed a longitudinal, noninvasive imaging-based approach using compatible platforms for studying mucormycosis infection. Our strategy integrates Galleria mellonella as an intermediate model, and a translational murine model, enabling systematic data collection across the experimental pipeline and strengthening the applicability of findings to human disease. The G. mellonella model provides a valuable and cost-effective platform for studying infections and screening potential therapeutics, and has been successfully utilized in fungal research, including studies on mucormycosis [29,30]. Complementing this are murine models, which provide closer physiological and immunological similarities to humans, offering greater translatability. To advance these efforts, we have bioengineered bioluminescent (BL) strains of Mucor lusitanicus, with optimized light emission and subsequently established both G. mellonella and a murine infection model incorporating micro-CT imaging for longitudinal assessment of host pathological changes. M. lusitanicus was chosen as a model organism as protocols to genetically modify this species are best described. Although M. lusitanicus is less frequently encountered clinically and exhibits lower pathogenicity than major Mucorales pathogens, it retains sufficient virulence in experimental models to demonstrate infection dynamics. As such, it represents an ideal starting point for the development of bioluminescent (BL) strains within the order Mucorales, providing a proof-of-concept framework that lays the foundation for a more comprehensive understanding of disease progression, supporting in-depth research into virulence, pathogenesis, therapeutic efficacy, and cross-species comparisons, accelerating translation of preclinical findings into human studies.

Strains and plasmids used in this study are listed in Table 1. All fungal strains used are taxonomically classified as M. lusitanicus, previously named as M. circinelloides var. lusitanicus. Growth media and conditions, spore harvesting and determination of spore concentration were carried out as described before [27]. Escherichia coli DH5α cells were used as host for plasmid propagation and grown in LB broth medium, supplemented with 0.1 mg/ml ampicillin if needed. Bacterial cultures were incubated at 37°C overnight.

First, a synthetic codon-optimized version of the firefly (Photinus pyralis) luciferase gene (without peroxisomal target sequence) was generated by back-translating the amino acid sequence into DNA sequence (http://genomes.urv.es/OPTIMIZER/), applying the Mucor lusitanicus codon usage table. Codon usage frequencies for M. circinelloides f. lusitanicus were obtained from the Codon Usage Database (NCBI-GenBank Release; kazusa.or.jp; http://www.kazusa.or.jp/codon/cgibin/showcodon.cgi?species=29924&aa=4&style=N) [32]. The codon-optimized luciferase sequence, flanked by XhoI and SacII restriction sites, was synthesized by GeneArt Gene Synthesis Service (Thermofisher, Germany) and subcloned into the standard vector pMAT, yielding the plasmid pMAT_luc_opt. To replicate higher light emission achieved in previous constructs [27], we generated plasmids containing the respective luciferase sequence under the control of either zinc permease zrt1 (ID 1,540,454; Mucor lusitanicus CBS277.49 vs 3; http://genome.jgi.doe.gov/Mucci3/Mucci3.home.html) [33] or the histone 3, his3 (ID 157,320, Mucor lusitanicus CBS277.49 vs 2; http://genome.jgi.doe.gov/Mucci2/Mucci2.home.html) [34] promoter and a functional leuA gene as selective marker, integrated in carRP (Figure S1). Targeted integration of the whole construct in the Mucor carRP gene was aimed to achieve easier identification of positive clones, as positive clones formed white colonies, due to disturbance of carotene biosynthesis, while those without integration had a yellow phenotype. As previously, strain R7B (leuA-) was used as the recipient strain. Generation of protoplasts and the transformation procedure were performed by electroporation as described before [27]. Positive transformants (white colonies) were repeatedly transferred to fresh selective agar plates (3–4 cycles) to obtain homokaryons, tested for light emission by luminometer, and checked by colony PCR. Therefore, site-specific integration of the fragment containing leuA, respective promoter and luciferase, was checked using a primer set flanking the integration site (carRP-ExtF1: 5´GGGCACATTGACGTAGAAGG, binding upstream of 5´ region and carp-ExtR1: 5´GCTGTTGCTGTGCTAACATCAT, binding downstream of 3´ region). PCR products were visualized by electrophoresis on a 0.8 % agarose gel. Integration was identified by a size shift of the PCR product from 4.6kb in the parental strain (R7B) and 9.6kb in the positive transformants (Figure S2). Briefly, 2 µg of DNA was digested overnight with 20 units of NcoI at 37°C, separated on a 0.8% agarose gel, transferred to nylon membrane, and hybridized with a DIG-labeled probe targeting the luciferase coding sequence.

sections.title: Characterization of generated strains in in vitro and in vivo systems in vitro characterization – luminometric assays

paragraphs.en: Three clones in each background were tested for light emission in a luminometric assay. Therefore, spores were harvested and grown as described previously [27]. Light emission was measured immediately after D-luciferin addition (10 mM, Synchem Germany) using a Varioscan Lux (Thermo Scientific, Germany) luminometer. Relative light units (RLUs) were normalized to the optical density of each microtiter well. In addition, light emission was imaged by a scientific-grade CCD camera (IVIS Lumina SII, Caliper Life Sciences, Hopkinton, USA). Clones with the highest and most consistent light emission were selected for further experiments. Light emission was then further assessed in relation to luciferin concentration. Strains were cultured in YNB medium in 96-well white plates (Nunc), and D-luciferin (Synchem, Germany) was added at final concentrations of 1, 2.5, 5, and 10 µM using automated dispensers. Luminescence was recorded using a kinetic protocol over 30 min, with one measurement per minute and a baseline reading prior to luciferin addition. For each strain and luciferin concentration, six technical replicates were included, and experiments were repeated in triplicate. To rule out differences in light emission caused by variations in growth of individual wells and/or strains, the same assay was carried out in a clear 96-well plate (Greiner), which allows for determining growth by OD620 measurement. The obtained values were then used for normalization of RLU values measured after injection of D-luciferin. In addition, the same microtiter plates were also processed for imaging analysis using the IVIS Lumina SII imaging system with open filter, F/stop1, subject height 2 cm, medium binning with a 10 s exposure time per image. Following image acquisition, the bioluminescent signal was quantified in radiance (p/sec/cm2/sr) using the region of interest (ROI) grid function and one ROI for the background area. Values were normalized by subtracting the background signal from each ROI of each well.

Sixth-instar Galleria mellonella (G. mellonella) larvae used in this study was obtained from Flotex GBR (Augsburg, Germany) and subsequently from an in-house laboratory-grade colony (KU Leuven, Belgium). The in-house colony was maintained under controlled environmental conditions, fed with an organic diet, and kept in a pesticide- and fungicide-free environment, as previously described [22,35].

To determine the suitability of our strains for in vivo studies, we performed an initial screening using G. mellonella larvae. Strains were cultured as described above and spores were harvested, filtered using pluriStrainer 40 µm cell strainers (pluriSelect, Leipzig, Germany) to remove hyphae and sporangiophores, and washed by centrifugation for 5 min at 2500 rpm, repeated three times. The spore concentration was determined using a hemocytometer and adjusted to 5 × 107 spores/ml in insect physiological saline (IPS) or saline. Sixth-instar larvae of G. mellonella (Flotex GBR, with an average weight of 0.5 g) were infected with 1 × 106 spores/larva (previously determined as an appropriate inoculum by [29]) by injecting 20 µl of the spore solution into the left rear pro-leg with a myjector insulin syringe (Terumo), followed by incubation at 37°C. The 20 μL volume was used during initial in vivo characterization (screening) of strains. Survival was monitored over 6 d and compared to survival curves of the parental strain R7B and to each other (20 larvae per group). From a separate batch, ten infected larvae were processed for BL imaging (BLI). At 48 h post-infection, surviving larvae exhibiting signs of infection (melanization, reduced motility) were injected with 60 µl of D-luciferin and gently rolled to ensure even distribution of the substrate throughout the body. Larvae were then placed in 12- or 6-well plates and incubated on ice for 5 min to immobilize them for image acquisition (effect of cold temperature on luciferase activity was evaluated previously in in vitro cultures and shown to have no effect). These procedures were designed to minimize artifacts and enable the recording of strain-specific BL signals at their full emission potential for reliable comparison. Experiments were repeated at least twice. Details of BLI acquisition and analysis are provided in the dedicated BLI Methods subsection below.

Healthy In-house-bred G. mellonella adult larvae (6th-instar larvae stage) with an average weight of approximately 350 mg were selected for the experiments. Larvae were randomly assigned to experimental groups (n = 6 per group; done in duplicate) and housed individually in 12-well plates. For infection, larvae were inoculated with 10 µl of spore suspension (concentration adjusted to volume to maintain equivalent inoculum dose) using a Hamilton syringe (31 gauge, Hamilton Company, Switzerland) via the last left proleg into the hemolymph with spore suspensions prepared as described above. This injection volume was chosen to accommodate multiple injections (infection, luciferin, treatments) when experimental design requires them while staying within safe limits for G. mellonella larvae. Following infection, larvae were kept at 37°C without food in a dark environment. Larvae’s health status was assessed longitudinally using an adapted health index scoring system (Table 2) [35].

The obtained daily scores were expressed and plotted in percentage of maximal health. Sham-infected larvae were used as controls. At the experimental endpoint or upon death, larvae were weighed and homogenized for subsequent fungal quantification by CFU plating, histology and ex vivo BLI analysis.

Animal studies were performed with authorization from the Ethics Committee for Animal Experimentation at KU Leuven (ECD project P067/2023) and in full accordance with national and European regulations. All animal experiments in this study were in accordance with the ARRIVE guidelines. Male and female 8–10-week-old C57BL/6 mice (Janvier Laboratories, France) were housed in individually ventilated cages (max five animals per cage [eight cages], separated by sex) with ad libitum access to food and water. Animals were randomly assigned to experimental groups. Before infection, mice were rendered neutropenic to model neutropenia as an underlying condition predisposing to mucormycosis. This was achieved through intraperitoneal (i.p.) injections of cyclophosphamide (0.9% saline solution; Sigma-Aldrich, Belgium) at a dose of 200 mg/kg of body weight on day −4, −1 and with a booster on day 2; day 0 was defined as the day of inoculation (infection). For immunosuppression analysis, blood was drawn by cardiac puncture and anticoagulated with 3.8% trisodium citrate (1 unit per 9 parts of blood) on day 0 (immunosuppression control = 2 male and 2 female mice; neutropenia verified before proceeding) and the rest on sacrifice/humane-endpoint day. Blood cell counts were measured in control (sham-infected) and infected mice using the Advia 2120i hematology system (Siemens Healthcare GmbH, Germany). Severe neutropenia was considered as a total count of <100 neutrophils/µl. On experimental day 0, following confirmation of immunosuppression in the control group, mice were anesthetized with 2% isoflurane (Piramal Healthcare, UK) in 100% O2 for inoculation. Once sedated, mice were inoculated with 20 µl fungal inoculum suspension according to inoculation dose group (2.5 × 103, 2.5 × 105 and 2.5 × 106 M. lusitanicus CII (=R7B-lucC) spores in saline solution) via an orotracheal route, as previously described [21,36]. Mice were monitored daily for body weight, overall health, and signs of respiratory distress throughout all experimental phases, in addition to longitudinal imaging readouts (micro-CT and bioluminescence; under isoflurane anesthesia) until a predefined experimental or humane endpoint was reached (≥20% weight loss, severe respiratory distress, or abnormal posture/immobility with lack of response to stimuli). Mice were sacrificed using a pentobarbital overdose delivered through an i.p. injection. At sacrifice day or humane endpoint, organs were harvested (lungs) for subsequent fungal quantification by CFU plating, histology and ex vivo BLI analysis.

Whole larva or mouse lungs were homogenized (Tissue Master homogenizer; Omni International, USA) in 1 ml or 600 µl saline solution, respectively, for fungal quantification by CFU plating. Homogenates were plated on Sabouraud (+ chloramphenicol) agar plates. Plates were incubated at 37°C and counted daily up to 5 d. CFU counts were expressed in log10 CFU counts per gram of lung tissue.

sections.title: In vivo bioluminescence imaging Single-timepoint characterization of bioluminescent signal

paragraphs.en: Bioluminescent signals were acquired using an IVIS Spectrum in vivo Imaging System and Living Image Software (formerly PerkinElmer, now Revvity, Shelton, CT, USA) under the following settings: open filter, f/stop 1, subject height 2 cm, medium binning, and an exposure time of 60 s per image. Signal intensities (radiance; p/sec/cm2/sr) were quantified using the region of interest (ROI) grid function for larvae, with one additional ROI placed in the background area. Normalization was performed by subtracting the background signal from each individual larval ROI.

Time-series longitudinal BLI scans were performed daily post-infection in both G. mellonella and mice. In the G. mellonella model, larvae were injected with 10 µl of D-luciferin (Goldbio, St Louis MO, USA) through the last prolegs (alternating left and right on subsequent timepoints) using a Hamilton syringe before scanning. A previously optimized luciferin dose of 40 µg/g per larva was utilized [35]. Subsequently, larvae were placed in a black 12-well plate to avoid signals overlapping between wells (IBL Baustoff + Labor Gmbh, Austria). Images were acquired using the IVIS Spectrum imaging system (Revvity, USA) and the manufacturer’s Living Image software (version 4.5.4) using the following parameters: open filter, F/stop1, subject height 0.5 cm, medium binning with a 30-s exposure time per image. Five minutes post-luciferin injection, the corresponding well plate (lid in place) was placed inside the heated chamber at 37°C and scanned for 5 min (5 frames in average) to capture maximum BL signal peak intensity detection (photon-flux per second) used for reporting, as determined by prior optimization data. Larvae total photon fluxes were measured from circular regions of interest (ROI) covering each well (2.5 cm × 2.5 cm) using the Living Image Software version 4.5.4 (Perkin Elmer, USA).

In mice, fur was removed from the chest area using a commercially available depilatory cream 3 days before infection to favor the detection of BL signals. Mice were injected i.p. with D-luciferin (dose 500 mg/kg). Subsequently, mice were anesthetized with isoflurane gas anesthesia as previously described. When sedated, mice were placed inside the IVIS spectrum imaging system chamber in a supine position and continued under anesthesia for image acquisition using the following parameters: open filter, F/stop 1, subject height 1.5 cm, medium binning with 60 s exposure time per image. Consecutive image frames were collected for approximately 15 min (15 frames in average) to detect peak BL signal intensity (photon-flux per second) used for reporting. BLI signals were quantified from a region of interest covering the lung area (2.5 cm width × 2.5 cm height) using the Living Image Software version.

For micro-CT image acquisition, mice were anesthetized using gas anesthesia and placed in a heated, small animal Bruker micro-CT scanner (Belgium). Micro-CT data acquisition was performed using the SkyScan 1278 software (Bruker, Belgium), utilizing the following scanning modes: 50 kV X-ray source, 1 mm aluminum X-ray filter, 350 µA current, voxel size 50 µm and 150 ms exposure time per projection. Scans were conducted with 0.9° rotational increments, averaging three consecutive frames per projection angle to enhance signal-to-noise ratio, as previously described [21,37]. A baseline scan was performed before infection (day-1) and daily after infection. Respiratory weighted micro-CT data were reconstructed, visualized, and processed using software provided by the manufacturer as previously described (NRecon-v1.6.10.4, Data Viewer-v1.5.2.4, and CTan-v1.16.3.0) [21,38]. An in-house developed deep learning model for automated lung segmentation and quantification was used to define micro-CT-derived biomarkers [39], including total lung volume (TLV), aerated lung volume (ALV), and non-aerated lung volume (NALV) from reconstructed images. Micro-CT cumulative clinical score assessment was performed from reconstructed images visual observations and semi-quantitatively scored as detailed in previous studies [21,23,38,40–42]. Briefly, at baseline scans, each image was assigned a score of zero. Subsequently, scores were adjusted daily based on the changes in pulmonary lesion development: an increase resulted in a score of +0.25, stabilization or no change received a score of 0, and improvement was scored at −0.25, resulting in a cumulative score (performed by two independent researchers).

Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism version 10.4.0. (GraphPad Software Inc., USA) or R packages tidyverse [43] and rstatix. Survival analysis was performed using the Log-rank (Mantel-Cox) test. For longitudinal data, either two-way ANOVA with Sidak’s multiple comparisons test or a generalized linear model (when variable group sizes resulted from larval mortality) was applied. Endpoint data were analyzed with one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s multiple comparisons test. To satisfy normality assumptions (Shapiro–Wilk test and Q–Q plots), radiance and CFU values were log-transformed. All graphs represent mean values ± SD. p values are indicated in the figure (above; for baseline/control comparison) or figure legends (lateral; for groups comparison) with significant differences when p: * <0.05, ** <0.01, *** <0.001, **** <0.0001. The number of animals in each experimental group is represented as (n).

sections.title: Light emission in luciferase-containing strains was strongly enhanced by codon optimization

paragraphs.en: M. lusitanicus serves as the model organism for genetic manipulation among the Mucormycetes and was chosen to generate a set of codon-optimized luciferase-harboring strains in which luciferase is under the control of different promoters. In this study, three plasmids were generated as a basis for transformation by homologous integration of a fragment containing codon-optimized (either for mammalian usage or specific for Mucor codon usage) firefly luciferase without peroxisomal target sequence. By integration in the carRP locus, carotene biosynthesis was disturbed, which facilitated screening for positive clones. For all three fragments, positive clones, validated by colony PCR (Figure S2) and Southern analysis (Figure S3A-B), were obtained and named R7B_lucA (Mucor optimized luciferase under the control of Pzrt1), R7B_lucB (mammalian optimized luciferase, Phis3) and R7B_lucC (Mucor optimized luciferase, Phis3). The previously generated strain R7B_luc [27] (mammalian optimized luciferase, Pzrt1) was used as a comparative control in validation assays. Selected transformants of the new strains showed normal growth and exhibited similar virulence potential in G. mellonella larvae, a prerequisite for our aim to build up useful model systems (Figure S4). Next, we evaluated the light emission of our new strains versus R7B_luc induced by different concentrations of D-luciferin. Independent of the luciferin concentration, the highest relative light units (RLUs) were detected in R7B_lucA, assuring our expectations that codon optimization does increase light emission significantly. R7B_lucA emitted 10.9–13.6 times more light than R7B_luc, with the highest signal in samples induced by 5 µM luciferin, whereas the fold increase in comparison to the non-optimized strain was highest (13.6x) at the lowest luciferin concentration used (0.5 µM). R7B_lucC, in which Mucor-codon optimized luciferase was controlled by Phis3, also showed higher RLUs than R7B_luc (1.1–1.9-fold increase), indicating that, also under relatively weaker induction, codon optimization has a positive effect. This is obvious when comparing the emission of strains with the same promoter -R7B_luc to R7B_lucA, or R7B_lucB to R7B_lucC (Figure 1(A), Figure S5A). To rule out differences in light emission based on biomass, all values were normalized to fungal growth (OD620 nm). Light signals were also shown to be strongly dependentent from luciferin concentrations, with the maximum peak for R7B_lucA at 5 µM, while for R7B_lucC the maximum was at 10 µM, although not statistically significant (Figure S5C). Time course experiments with 5 μM of luciferin, which gave the highest light signal, showed that the light emission declined after the maximum peak, which was seen in the first measurement after luciferin addition in all strains. Nevertheless, in all strains signals were detected throughout the duration of 30 min, indicating the signal is stable enough for the time needed to monitor light expression in vivo (Figure 1(B)).

To ensure that strain-dependent light emission was sufficient to be detectable with our imaging platform, we additionally imaged the same plate using the IVIS Spectrum system, revealing the same significant differences between the strains in which luciferase is under control of zrt1 promoter. In strains where light expression is controlled by his3 promoter, statistically higher light emission was only detected at 10 µM luciferin (Figure S5A). Independent of the device used, R7B_lucA clearly resulted in the highest light emission (Figure S5B).

sections.title: Promoter activity differs between in vitro and in vivo imaging

paragraphs.en: Next, all four luciferase-harboring strains were compared for their ability to produce detectable light in in vivo, with characterization performed in G. mellonella larvae imaged 48 h post-infection. Light signals were visualized and measured in all infected larvae only when they were infected with Mucor-codon-optimized strains (R7B_lucA and R7B_lucC), whereas the mammalian-optimized versions did not produce detectable light (Figure 2(A,B)–). Surprisingly, overall higher signals, although not statistically significant, were detected in larvae infected with the R7B_lucC strain, in which luciferase is controlled by Phis3, the histone H3 promoter, than when controlled by Pzrt1, controlling a putative zinc permease known to be differentially expressed according to zinc availability. This trend was the opposite of what we expected according to in vitro results (Figure 1, Figure S5). This indicates that promoter selection is critical and also shows the importance of using in vivo pre-screening of BL strains, as in vitro results might lead to different results.

sections.title: Sensitive real-time in vivo mucormycosis burden quantification via BLI in G. mellonella

paragraphs.en: Following in vitro and in vivo characterization, we aimed to establish a longitudinal, imaging-compatible G. mellonella infection model for mucormycosis research. To achieve this, we assessed the sensitivity of BLI in detecting fungal burden and evaluated two M. lusitanicus strains (R7B_lucA_II = AII and R7B_lucC_II = CII) to determine which can provide the most sensitive and reproducible BL signals for quantitative in vivo imaging across a range of inoculum burdens over time. Larvae were infected with either 1 × 103, 1 × 104, 1 × 105 and 1 × 106 spores (M. lusitanicus AII or CII) and followed up over a time course of 5 d; initial scan 20 min after infection (0 hr). For both strains, the highest inoculation dose (1 × 106) showed a significant decrease in health and survival compared to intermediate (1 × 104 and 1 × 105; Figure 3(A,B,D-E)–) and low inoculation dose groups (1×103; Figure S7A-B). In this experiment (n = 6 larvae per group), it seemed that AII was more virulent, as indicated by more severe clinical deterioration and higher mortality by day 3 (mortality: AII, 83% [5/6] versus CII, 50% [3/6]); however, this apparent difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.0943). Consistently, in a larger experiment including 60 larvae (Figure S4), no significant differences in virulence potential were observed between strains.

BLI capabilities of our M. lusitanicus AII and CII strains in vivo demonstrated a peak in photon flux at day 1 in the two highest inoculation groups relative to sham-infected controls (Figure 3(C,F)), with the highest inoculum dose (1 × 106) exhibiting a statistically significant increase; representative BLI images for this group are shown in Figure 3(G). The peaks were followed by a progressive decline in signal intensity over time in both inoculated groups. At an inoculum of 1 × 105 spores, larvae exhibited BL signals of lower magnitude, while retaining the characteristic day-1 peak in photon flux followed by a gradual decline, consistent with the kinetics observed at higher inoculation doses. In contrast, no distinct peaks were observed in the two lowest inoculation groups (1 × 104 [Figure 3(C,F)] and 1 × 103 [Figure S7C]), with photon flux values remaining comparable across groups, precluding meaningful differentiation. Nevertheless, BL signals persisted across the observation period, although with a progressive decline in intensity, reaching levels comparable to sham-infected controls by the end. When comparing the BL emission capabilities between strains across all inoculation doses, larvae infected with the CII strain exhibited higher BL signal intensities than those infected with the AII strain, most notably at the highest inoculation dose, where signals from CII-infected larvae were significantly higher than those from AII-infected ones (p = 0.0045). Moreover, the BL signal from the highest inoculation CII group remained consistently detectable throughout the entire observation period, demonstrating its sensitivity for longitudinal in vivo tracking.

Ex vivo BL signals from larvae homogenates were likewise observed in the highest inoculation groups (1 × 105 and 1 × 106), correlating to the initial inoculation size but only in M. lusitanicus CII-infected larvae (Figure S7D, F). CFU counts support the BLI observations, confirming the presence of fungal burden. Yet, CFUs could not be recovered from the two lower inoculation groups and were detectable in only half of the cases in the higher inoculation groups (1 × 105 and 1 × 106), yielding low fungal burdens. Moreover, the method was not sensitive enough to distinguish significant differences between groups (Figure S7E, G). The minimal or absent CFU recovery, along with the lack of inoculum-based group differentiation, is likely due to low fungal burdens and to the fragility of Mucorales hyphae during mechanical homogenization. Indeed, histological analysis at the end point revealed limited fungal structures and granulomas, supporting the notion that the infection is being contained at the cost of clinical deterioration (Figure S7H). Consistent findings from independent BLI experiments at two of our research centers (Figure 2 and 3, and Figure S6) demonstrated that the M. lusitanicus CII strain exhibited superior bioluminescent performance, characterized by higher signal intensity and a broad dynamic range, allowing detection at low fungal burdens. Based on these properties, CII was selected for further investigation in deep-seated infections in mice.

sections.title: Bioluminescence and micro-CT as complementary longitudinal tools for assessing fungal burden and host responses in murine mucormycosis

paragraphs.en: Our next aim was to establish the first longitudinal and multimodal imaging-compatible murine model of mucormycosis infection, combining BLI to quantify fungal burden with micro-CT to assess host–pathogen interactions in neutropenic mice, a high-risk condition for Mucorales infection. We evaluated whether the CII strain could support improved imaging and quantification of pulmonary fungal burden. For this, 8–10-week-old male and female mice were rendered neutropenic (cyclophosphamide-induced). Upon confirming immunosuppression in control mice (<100 neutrophils/µl), mice were infected with either 2.5 × 103, 2.5 × 105 and 2.5 × 106 spores (n = 10 per group; 5 males and 5 females) and compared for survival, health score, in vivo and ex vivo BLI, and micro-CT readouts over 4 days post-infection, with each male and female data pooled as no significant sex-related differences were observed (Table S1). All mice lost comparable weight upon infection, regardless of inoculum dose (Figure S8A). The weight loss was more pronounced on days 2–3 post-infection (moderate toward severe), while a slight recovery in weight was observed on day 4. Differences in infection severity due to initial fungal burden were not evident from weight loss or survival between infected groups (Figure S8A–B). In contrast, BLI provided a more sensitive readout, revealing inoculum-dependent differences in photon flux over time and thereby demonstrating its utility for capturing dynamic fungal growth, a critical determinant of disease progression (Figure 4(A–B)). By day 1 post-infection, the highest inoculum already showed a significant increase in signals relative to baseline scans (Figure 4(B)). Notably, on day 4 post-infection, a decline in BLI signal intensity was observed in the two highest inoculum groups (2.5 × 105 and 2.5 × 106), corresponding with a slight increase in body weight, suggestive of a possible fungal load decrease or infection containment. Indeed, histological analysis revealed limited hyphal presence, with fungal structures confined to sparse granuloma-like formations and immune cell infiltration persisting despite severe neutropenia, likely driven by tissue-resident cells (Figure S8C). Fungal burden assessed by CFU counts could not be determined in the lowest inoculation group and was largely undetectable in the higher groups (2.5 × 105: 2/8 mice; 2.5 × 106: 2/8 mice; Figure S8D). Ex vivo BLI of lung homogenates indicated slightly higher sensitivity, particularly in the two highest inoculum groups, but the effect was mild and not statistically significant, most likely due to hyphal breakage and loss of signal from non-viable elements during homogenization (Figure S8E). However, detection was inconsistent, and no significant differences were observed between groups, which may be explained by the susceptibility of fungal hyphae to mechanical disruption during homogenization. Taken together, BLI once again demonstrated evidence for fungal burden quantification in vivo, offering a direct, real-time, and previously inaccessible assessment in deep-seated infections (lung infection) in mice.

Next, we employed micro-CT imaging to investigate pulmonary host tissue responses to infection, complementing fungal burden assessment with pathological insights into lesion development. Semi-quantitative analysis from visual clinical assessment (Figure 4(C)) of micro-CT scans for lung lesion development revealed an increase in the severity of pneumonia over time (Figure 4(D)). Significant changes were detected from day 2 in the two highest inoculation groups and from day 4 in the lowest inoculation group, compared to baseline scans (Figure 4(D)). Quantitative analysis of Micro-CT lung tissue lesion development (non-aerated volume), revealed an increase compared to baseline (pre-infection) as early as day 1 post-infection, followed by a slight decrease on days 3 and 4 for the two highest inocula (Figure 4(E)); yet increases were only significant for the intermediate inoculum (2.5 × 105) group on day 2. Aerated lung volume (ALV), representing the air-filled portion of the lungs, displayed an initial rise in the two highest inoculum groups during the first 2 d before stabilizing (Figure S8F). Whereas ALV normally decreases as pneumonia progresses and air spaces are replaced by lesions, the observed increase likely reflects compensatory hyperinflation in response to infection-driven air displacement, entrapment, or early lesion development.

The modest changes observed in ALV are consistent with the strong compensatory capacity of mice [44,45], yet micro-CT was sensitive enough to detect them. In the lowest inoculum group, both aerated and non-aerated volumes increased only on day 4, implying a more gradual disease onset.

In this study, we present a novel, versatile preclinical approach that expands current experimental approaches to study mucormycosis by integrating innovative tools and models to advance our understanding of mucorales infections and therapeutic evaluations. This includes the establishment of the first bioluminescent Mucorales strain, namely M. lusitanicus, optimized for both in vitro and in vivo applications, and the introduction of a G. mellonella model as a high-throughput BLI-based infection system and bridge for early-stage and mammalian studies. Complementing these models, we developed a murine model approach for investigating infection dynamics, host tissue responses and antifungal efficacy, integrating longitudinal real-time imaging that combines BLI for fungal burden assessment with micro-CT for detailed spatial characterization of host responses.

By developing an optimized bioluminescent M. lusitanicus and applying BL imaging, we address a critical gap in Mucorales research by presenting a methodological framework for reliable fungal burden quantification, which has long been hindered by the failure of CFU enumeration. CFU counts are single-timepoint readouts commonly used for fungal burden and disease assessment [19]. However, this methodology comes with several limitations. Fungi of the order Mucorales are distinguished by having a thin-walled aseptate mycelium that easily fragments during tissue homogenization [7,46]. Combined with the inherent reduced culture positivity in samples, often less than 50% [7,46], these limitations render CFU counts as a suboptimal method for assessing fungal burden in Mucorales infections, a limitation that was also corroborated in our in vivo experimental platforms. Alternatively, qPCR offers a potential approach for quantifying fungal burden [47], as hyphal fragility may not be a major limitation to affect DNA-based measurements. However, multiple studies have reported that fungal qPCR is affected by variability in sampling procedures, tissue processing, and extraction methods, resulting in inconsistent DNA recovery [47,48]. BL imaging is not subject to these specific limitations. While we did not perform a direct comparison of sensitivity or quantitative performance, the two approaches are likely complementary, with qPCR potentially offering higher analytical sensitivity and BLI enabling longitudinal and spatial assessment of infection dynamics. Histology, when yielding quantitative data, can provide insights into fungal burden and host responses in tissues. Nevertheless, it is also constrained by factors such as single-timepoint assessment, sampling bias, and the need for expertise to accurately interpret morphological changes.

The development of the first bioluminescent M. lusitanicus strain suitable for in vivo experiments marks a critical advancement in Mucorales research by (1) tackling the long-standing challenges of genetic manipulation in this order [49,50] (2) enabling its application for real-time, longitudinal monitoring of infection dynamics in vivo, and (3) overcoming the limitations of endpoint tools such as CFUs for fungal burden quantification. M. lusitanicus is widely considered as a reference model within the Mucorales order for genetic studies, recognized for its extensive genetic toolkit that has driven significant advancements in genetic manipulation and cellular process dissection. While it is not among the most clinically prevalent or virulent Mucorales species, M. lusitanicus produces measurable infection in experimental models, making it a practical choice for methodological and preclinical studies. Within our group, an initial attempt to bioengineer a Mucorales BL strain was done through the transformation of M. lusitanicus with a firefly luciferase gene [27]. Even though the results were optimal for in vitro assessments, the transformant was not suitable for in vivo imaging [51]. Therefore, to enhance reporter sensitivity, we introduced a codon-optimized version of luciferase, which, as expected, led to improved light emission, similar to what has been shown for A. fumigatus [21,51] and C. albicans strains [52] thereby facilitating fungal burden quantification in vitro and the real-time longitudinal follow-up of fungal burden in our G. mellonella and neutropenic mouse model of infection. Interestingly, throughout the validation of our BL strains in G. mellonella, it became evident that in vitro characterization alone is insufficient to predict the in vivo applicability of generated strains. While the M. lusitanicus AII strain exhibited higher BL signals in vitro, this did not translate to our in vivo G. mellonella model, where the CII strain demonstrated superior performance, most likely due to the influence of the selected promoter and its regulatory effects in vivo. Pzrt1 encodes a zinc transporter regulated by zinc availability and strongly expressed in zinc-deficient conditions, a state expected in the host, known as nutritional immunity. On the other hand, histone H3 expression in actively growing hyphae is expected to be more stable and regulated by epigenetic mechanisms rather than by nutritional components [33,52]. As we did not study expression patterns in detail by other means than measuring light emission, we can only hypothesize that lower light levels in our in vitro assays are connected to the age of the culture. Reaching the stationary phase in the 96-well plates potentially goes in hand with reduced histone expression [53]. Our results further underscore the utility of our G. mellonella model as a screening platform, minimizing additional mouse experiments, with their ethical implications, and emphasizing the need to always validate newly developed BL strains for in vivo use.

Taken together, our observations support the use of our novel BL CII strain and BL imaging approach as a sensitive and quantitative tool for assessing fungal burden. This strategy not only enables in vitro applications such as antifungal efficacy testing, leveraging the exclusive BL signal produced by viable fungi, but also supports in vivo longitudinal monitoring of fungal burden, including in deep-seated infections, such as pulmonary disease in mice. Indeed, BL imaging was sensitive enough to detect dose-dependent fungal burden variations and temporal monitoring of mucormycosis infection in both G. mellonella and mice. For instance, in our mouse model, BL imaging allowed for the follow-up on fungal burden as early as day 1 after infection in the highest inoculation group, providing crucial longitudinal data throughout the entire course of infection. As such, our approach demonstrated high sensitivity in detecting fungal burden variations within groups over time (e.g. decline on day 4), and differences in fungal burdens between inoculation groups, reinforcing its value for real-time infection monitoring. The achievement of our BL M. lusitanicus early fungal detection capabilities is on par with the capabilities of A. fumigatus and C. neoformans strains, which have redefined fungal infection research [21–23,35,38,41,50], thereby unlocking comparable potential to advance mucormycosis research. Extending this approach to ex vivo applications, our findings indicate that BL imaging may offer greater sensitivity for fungal burden detection in infected larvae and lung homogenates, in contrast to the limited utility of CFU counts. However, its interpretation remains constrained by hyphal mechanical disruption during tissue homogenization, though it may serve as a semiquantitative or indirect indicator of fungal infection.

A comprehensive understanding of infection extends beyond fungal burden alone, as virulence and host responses are equally critical determinants of disease progression and patient outcomes. In our G. mellonella and murine models of mucormycosis, we use a multimodal approach to capture and complement fungal dynamics and elucidate host responses. Histological assessment provides valuable insights into host responses, yet its endpoint nature and labor-intensive analysis highlight the need for complementary longitudinal readouts for dynamic assessment. Survival and health scoring in G. mellonella provide a noninvasive approach for assessing infection severity through a semi-quantitative evaluation of clinical deterioration based on movement, melanization, and cocoon formation. These parameters serve as indirect indicators of the physiological impact of the fungal infection on the host and are recognized as a reliable proxy for virulence assessment and host fitness in the field [22,29,30,35,54].

In our G. mellonella model, BL analysis suggested a progressive decrease in fungal burden and infection containment 1 d after infection. The proposition that host-immune responses were effectively containing the fungi was further supported by endpoint histological analysis, revealing melanized granuloma-like structures with contained fungal structures in infected larvae, a common immune response in G. mellonella to pathogens [55]. However, we observed a progressive decrease in health and survival probabilities over time across all inoculation doses despite the decrease in fungal burden. Interestingly, despite infection containment, the elucidated immune activation appears to have negatively impacted the overall larval health, as reflected by these host biomarkers. These findings highlight the importance of our complementary approach, as relying solely on these host-response readouts could have led to the assumption that infection severity and host deterioration were driven as a response to increasing fungal burden and not due to deregulated host responses. However, these biomarkers are subjective and provide only limited insight into host–pathogen interactions, including tissue damage, inflammation, and structural changes.

We successfully overcame this limitation in our murine model by implementing micro-CT imaging, a powerful tool that combines high-resolution imaging with quantitative assessment of host responses to mucormycosis. This approach provided a comprehensive real-time assessment of lesion development, such as lung lesions, capturing their type, extent, and structural impact while detecting changes in air volume and tissue density from infection onset to the experimental endpoint [21,37,44,56]. Based on other assessed biomarkers, including survival, health score and BLI, our analysis suggests a progressive increase in infection, followed by containment on the final day, as indicated by clinical improvement and decreased BL signals. However, these measures alone did not shed light on the host response (lesions) elicited by the fungus. With our micro-CT biomarkers, we were able to detect in real-time the increasing development of lung lesion volume in all groups (non-aerated volume) and in aerated volume, most likely secondary to air entrapment, followed by relative stabilization in the following days, correlating with the observed recovery in health and decrease in fungal burden. Of note, despite the expectation that immunosuppression would markedly diminish host responses, lesions were still observed, likely reflecting the contribution of resident immune cells at the infection site, which are less affected by cyclophosphamide, as confirmed by histological analysis. Complementary immunosuppression regimens, such as corticosteroid treatment, could be used to impair resident immune cell function or further favor hyphal growth [19,57]. Visual assessment of lung pathology through cumulative lesion analysis provided semiquantitative insights into disease progression, capturing both the temporal increase in lesion number and severity as well as the emergence of features such as mucus accumulation, consolidation, airway dilation, and atelectasis. Notably, this biomarker continued to increase when others stabilized, reflecting a potential discrepancy. This divergence may be explained by the persistence of CT-detectable lesions such as consolidations, which can outlast symptom onset due to ongoing inflammation and fibrosis, with resolution requiring extended tissue repair [58]. Similarly, the observed discrepancy with lung lesion volume may stem from the compensatory capacity of mice to maintain lung volumes despite underlying structural damage [44].

In summary, we address a major limitation of current mucormycosis research by overcoming the constraints of single‑endpoint invasive methodologies through the establishment of a robust, imaging‑driven preclinical framework validated in M. lusitanicus. Our preclinical approach integrates in vitro, G. mellonella, and mouse models, each offering distinct advantages in assessing infection progression and host responses. By combining BL imaging for real‑time fungal burden tracking with micro‑CT for high‑resolution characterization of host pathology, the platform achieves continuous, non‑invasive monitoring and delivers a versatile multimodal system to advance mechanistic insights and support the translational evaluation of antifungal strategies in future studies. The creation of the first bioluminescent Mucorales strain enabling true in vivo bioluminescence imaging further establishes a genetic approach that can be directly transferred to more virulent species, including Mucor circinelloides, Rhizopus microsporus, and Rhizopus arrhizus, positioning this system for rapid expansion toward clinically relevant pathogens. Altogether, the applications of our platform are numerous and will empower researchers to gain deeper insights into the underlying mechanisms regulating mucormycosis pathogenesis, co-infection models, virulence studies, antifungal resistance, and novel therapeutic candidates, including new compounds and immune therapies.

figures.caption: In vivo bioluminescence reveals promoter-dependent differences among codon-optimized M. lusitanicus strains. Comparative bioluminescence of G. mellonella larvae infected with 1 × 106 spores of codon-optimized M. lusitanicus strains 48 h post-infection. A) Representative images of infected larvae following injection of 60 µl of 10 mM D-luciferin (IVIS Spectrum in vivo Imaging System, PerkinElmer). figures.label: Figure 3.
figures.caption: Novel bioluminescent M. lusitanicus strains enable real-time monitoring of mucormycosis infection in G. mellonella. G. mellonella larvae were infected with M. lusitanicus AII or CII bioluminescent (BL) strains to compare BL signal emission and infection progression. Inoculum doses ranging from 1 × 103 to 1 × 106 spores were used to assess inoculum-dependent dynamics (1 × 103 shown in Figure S7A–C). A, D) Longitudinal health scores (Table 2) provided an index of infection severity (% decrease). B, E) survival curves of larvae post-infection, highlighting mortality rates over time according to inoculum. C, F) Quantitative analysis of light emission signals from larvae (total flux) over time and G) representative BLI images comparison from each experimental bioluminescent strain-group (1 × 106 inoculum; n = 6). Statistical analysis was performed using two-way ANOVA with Sidak’s multiple comparisons test, assessing differences between groups over time (lateral comparisons on legends) and relative to sham-infected per time point (significance markers above curves; color denotes the group exhibiting significant differences). Longitudinal data were evaluated on day 3. Survival data were analyzed using a log-rank (Mantel-Cox) test. Statistical significance is indicated as p ≤ *p ≤ 0.05, **p ≤ 0.01, ***p ≤ 0.001, ****p ≤ 0.0001.

figures.label: Figure 4.
figures.caption: Real-time in vivo imaging of fungal burden and host responses after mucormycosis infection.
